libraries.group: Structures, functional programming and the type system
Files, archives and the operating system

modules.brief: Find what the agent can call, and take a documentation view back out of the window.
modules.detail:
The system prompt names modules and no function at all, so this module is the way into every other one: `search` turns a keyword or a module id into fully-qualified names, and `views.open_docs_view` reads one of those names in full.

Searching is bound in every program whatever a run enables, because an agent must always be able to find the functions it does hold. Closing a documentation view is the exception and is bought by a capability: opening one only ever appends to the prompt, while closing one rewrites its middle, and a run that did not enable it gets `ToolErrorCode.UNAVAILABLE`.

modules.brief: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace.
modules.detail:
Reading is the cheap direction of this sandbox and writing is the expensive one, so a program that reads a dozen files to decide what to change is well shaped, while one that rewrites forty large files in a single turn will exhaust its fuel budget.

Nothing here places anything in the agent's context window. `views.open_file` is the call that does.

modules.brief: Run shell commands in the workspace.
modules.detail:
One function, and the way a program reaches everything gg has no tool for: a build, a test run, `git`, `curl`, a package manager. The workspace is the working directory.

A non-zero exit is a *result* rather than a failure, because deciding whether a build or a test run passed is the single most common thing a program does with one.

modules.brief: The epic and issue board, on which work is decomposed into dispatchable units.
modules.detail:
An issue is heavyweight and self-contained: its scope, non-scope and completion criteria are exactly what a delegated child agent is briefed from, which is why `create_issue` asks for more than `tasks.add_task` does. Its five required arguments are positional, and Python lets a program pass any of them by name, which is what a call with this many strings in it should do.

Two of an issue's patch fields are three-way, and both take the same shape: leaving the argument out keeps what is there, `None` clears or detaches, and a value replaces or regroups.

modules.brief: A private task list, kept as a directed acyclic graph rather than as a list of lines.
modules.detail:
Every task may name the tasks that must finish before it, and an edge that would close a cycle is refused.

One spelling here is worth reading twice. A task's description is a three-way edit, and Python already spells two of the three: leaving the argument out keeps what is there, `None` clears it, and a string replaces it. `gg.core.UNCHANGED` is the name of the first, for a program that spells it out.

modules.brief: Durable memories, which survive a context compaction.
modules.detail:
A run picks one of three memory strategies and binds only that strategy's functions, so what this module offers is the honest answer to what memory can do here. The scratchpad keeps every memory in the context window (`write_memory`, `update_memory`); the two file-shaped strategies keep the contents outside it (`create_memory`, `read_memory`, `edit_memory`), one behind an index that is always in context and one behind `search_memories`. `delete_memory` is bound under all three.

Every mutation hands back the budget after it, so a program can decide whether to write another memory by reading numbers rather than by parsing a sentence about them.

The three writes take their fields as arguments rather than as a record. The membrane declares one `memory-input` for all of them, and a language whose optional arguments are keyword arguments has no reason to make a program construct a value before it can make a call.

modules.brief: Show a file, a computed value, or a function's documentation.
modules.detail:
A view is the only way material enters the agent's context window.

Under responses as code a whole program's output would otherwise collapse into one anonymous blob of logs, charged to one band, attributable to nothing and closable by nothing. A view restores what tool calling gave for free: one message per view, carrying the band it is charged to and the selector it can be closed by.

A program's own output is unreadable by the model that wrote it, and a view is the only way a value it computed reaches that model — `print` reaches nobody the program can hear back from.

modules.brief: Manage the agent's own context window.
modules.detail: These are the only calls whose effect is on the conversation rather than on the workspace. They are worth making from a program precisely because a program can decide *when* to: read a set of files, extract what matters, then evict the views, all in one turn.

modules.brief: Delegate work to child agents, and hand this session's own turn to another agent.
modules.detail:
`wait_for_subagents` can dominate a turn's wall clock — it blocks while real agents run — and the run's budget keeps ticking while it does. A program should therefore spawn broadly and wait once, rather than spawn-and-wait in a loop.

The brief is the one place this SDK enforces an "exactly one of" the native tool-calling schema can only check at dispatch: a child is briefed either with a self-contained `prompt` or with a board `issue_id`, both of them keyword arguments, and the wrapper refuses "neither" and "both" by name rather than letting the membrane's variant decide which one it saw first.

modules.brief: Read the skills this run authored.
modules.detail: A skill name is a plain string rather than an enum of the run's skills, because the catalogue is per-run while this component is baked once. The names available are listed in the system prompt, and an unknown one comes back as `not-found` carrying the full list.

modules.brief: Fetch a program that already ran, and hand a patched copy back to be run.
modules.detail:
Under responses as code a reply is a whole program, so a one-character mistake in a sixty-line program costs the sixty lines again. The library makes the fix proportional to the mistake: fetch what ran, patch it with ordinary string work, hand it back.

```python
source = programs.get()
programs.rerun(source.replace("improt", "import"))
```

modules.brief: End the session, with the ending that belongs to this agent's role.
modules.detail:
Under responses as code every reply is a program, so there is no prose turn that could mean "the work is done" — a model that answers "task complete" has written a reply that failed to be a program, not an ending. These are the calls that mean it, and a run binds only the group its agent's role has: an agent doing work gets `finish`, and a reviewer gets `approve` and `request_changes` instead.

None of them stops the program. Whatever follows an ending still runs, so an ending belongs last — and a program that then fails has its ending revoked along with everything else it decided.

modules.brief: The types every other module's signatures name: how a call fails, and what a patch leaves alone.
modules.detail:
A capability module owns the types it produces, so `FileRead` belongs to `gg.files` and `IssueCreated` to `gg.board`. The three here belong to none of them because they belong to all of them: every function in this SDK raises `ToolError`, and `UNCHANGED` is the default of every patch argument that can also be cleared.

They are also the names a program writes unqualified. `gg.scope` binds them directly into a program's namespace, because an `except` clause that had to spell out a module would be an `except` clause nobody writes.

functions.name: search
functions.brief: Search every function and type the agent can call, by keyword and by filter.
functions.detail:
This is how a name is found. Matching is a case-insensitive substring over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `open_docs_view`. Ranking is by the kind of evidence that matched — an entry whose own name matched outranks one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph — and a weaker kind never overtakes a stronger one however often it occurs.

Only entries this run bound are returned, so nothing a search finds is something the run withheld. The filters compose with each other and with `query`.

The page comes back as a value and is also opened as a view, under the selector `search results`, so it can be read on the next turn without a program showing it to itself. The next search replaces that view: it names what is being worked from rather than keeping a record.

Returns: The page that matched, best first. `total` counts every entry that matched before paging, so a page shorter than `total` is a page there is more of.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for an empty query with no filter at all — nothing matched and nothing was asked for are different answers — and for a `limit` of zero, which would ask for a page that answers nothing. A `module` or `type` that names something gg does not hold is not among them: it matches nothing.

signatures.signature: search(query: str, *, module: str | None = None, type: str | None = None, kind: DocKind | None = None, offset: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> DocSearch

parameters.name: query
parameters.doc: The words to match, as a case-insensitive substring. It may be empty when at least one filter is given.

parameters.name: module
parameters.doc: One module's id — `files`, `views`, `docs` — matched exactly. An empty `query` with a module is that module's whole directory rather than a search. A name no module has matches nothing rather than failing, so an empty page means the filter found nothing, not that it was rejected.

parameters.name: type
parameters.doc: One type's name, narrowing to that type and to the functions that take or return it. Like `module`, a name nothing declares matches nothing rather than failing.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.doc: Whether to return functions or types. The default returns both.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.doc: How many hits to skip, for reading past the first page. The default starts at the best hit.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.doc: The most hits to return. The default is gg's own page size and there is a ceiling above it, so comparing `len(hits)` against `total` is the only way to see a capped page. Zero is refused rather than read as "no cap".

functions.name: close
functions.brief: Take one documentation view out of the context window, by the key it was opened under.
functions.detail:
The removal has no cascade: closing a type's view leaves every function view beside it, and closing a function's leaves its types. Nothing records why a view was opened, so a type that is closed is opened again by the next function that mentions it.

Returns: How many views were taken away; a key that is not open closes `0` rather than failing.

Raises `ToolError`: `unavailable` under a run that did not enable closing documentation views.

parameters.name: key
parameters.doc: The fully-qualified name the view was opened under.

functions.name: close_all
functions.brief: Take every documentation view out of the context window.
functions.detail:
The blanket form of `close`, on exactly the same terms and behind the same capability.

Returns: How many documentation views went, and `0` rather than a failure when none was open.

Raises `ToolError`: `unavailable` under a run that did not enable closing documentation views.

functions.name: read_file
functions.brief: Read a file, as either a `TextFile` or an `ImageFile`.
functions.detail:
Which of the two comes back is detected from the file's bytes, never from the extension, so a mislabelled picture is still a picture. The two are ordinary classes, so an ordinary `match` narrows them:

```python
match files.read_file("logo.png"):
    case TextFile(contents=text):
        views.open_text("logo", text)
    case ImageFile(label=label):
        views.open_text("logo", label)
```

A relative path resolves against the workspace; an absolute one is read as given, so anything else in this container — an offloaded command's output under `/tmp/gg-shell`, say — is readable. This call hands bytes to the program and places nothing in the context window; reading a picture describes it and shows nothing, so a file only read here is a file nobody has looked at.

Returns: The `TextFile` for a text file's window, or the `ImageFile` describing a picture whose bytes never entered the program.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for a missing path.

signatures.signature: read_file(path: str, *, offset: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> FileRead

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to read, relative to the workspace or absolute.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.doc: The 1-based line to start at. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.doc: How many lines to return from `offset`. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

functions.name: read_text_file
functions.brief: Read a text file and hand back its contents directly.
functions.detail:
`read_file` without the narrowing, for the common case: the same read, the same window, the same cost.

Returns: The file's text, or the window of it a capped read policy allowed.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` when the path names a picture, which `read_file` inspects instead and `views.open_file` displays.

signatures.signature: read_text_file(path: str, *, offset: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> str

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to read, relative to the workspace or absolute.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.doc: The 1-based line to start at. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.doc: How many lines to return from `offset`. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

functions.name: write_file
functions.brief: Write UTF-8 text to a file, creating parent directories and replacing what is there.
functions.detail:
Writing is the expensive direction of this sandbox: rewriting more than a few dozen large files in one program exhausts its fuel budget, so a large rewrite is best split across several turns.

Returns: How many bytes were written, which is the UTF-8 length rather than the number of characters.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for an empty path, and `io-error` when creating the parent directories or the write itself failed.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: Where to write, relative to the workspace or absolute. Parent directories are created.

parameters.name: contents
parameters.doc: The UTF-8 text to write. It replaces the file entirely.

functions.name: edit_file
functions.brief: Replace the one exact occurrence of some text in a file with something else.
functions.detail:
Widening the surrounding context until the match is unique is the way to disambiguate; counting occurrences is not.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` when the text does not appear, and `conflict` — with the number of matches — when it appears more than once.

signatures.signature: edit_file(path: str, old_string: str, new_string: str) -> None

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to edit.

parameters.name: old_string
parameters.doc: The exact text to find, whitespace included. It must appear exactly once.

parameters.name: new_string
parameters.doc: The text to put in its place. An empty string deletes the match.

functions.name: list_dir
functions.brief: List a directory, sorted by name; the default lists the workspace root.
functions.detail:
Returns: One entry per name, sorted by name, and an empty list for an empty directory rather than a failure. Each `name` is bare, so joining it with the directory that was listed is what makes a path.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for a directory that is not there, and `invalid-argument` for a path that is given but empty — the default is what lists the workspace root.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The directory to list, relative to the workspace or absolute. The default lists the workspace root.

functions.name: shell
functions.brief: Run a command with `sh -c` in the workspace and hand back its merged stdout and stderr.
functions.detail:
A non-zero exit is not a failure: read `exit_code` on the result. Only a process that could not be launched, or one the timeout killed, raises.

This run may **offload** shell output — the `shell` tool's own description says which mode is in force. Under `offload`, `output` holds only the tail that fits and ends with a note naming the two files the command's full stdout and stderr were written to. Under `adaptive`, the default, a command that succeeded returns no output at all, only that note, and one that failed returns the tail. Grepping the named files is cheaper than re-running the command.

Returns: The command's merged stdout and stderr, its `exit_code` — `None` when a signal killed the process — and whether gg's cap `truncated` the output.

Raises `ToolError`: `limit-exceeded` when the timeout killed the process, and `io-error` when it could not be launched.

signatures.signature: shell(command: str, *, timeout_secs: float | None = None) -> ShellOutput

parameters.name: command
parameters.doc: The command line, run by `sh -c` with the workspace as its working directory.

parameters.name: timeout_secs
parameters.doc: How long to let it run, in seconds, before killing it. The default is gg's own 120, clamped to whatever is left of the run's wall-clock budget.

functions.name: create_epic
functions.brief: Create an epic to group related issues.
functions.detail:
`prefix` is 3-6 letters naming the epic; it is upper-cased and becomes the epic's id, which is also what its issues are numbered from — a prefix of `auth` gives issues `AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2`, and so on.

Returns: The id the prefix resolved to, and the board budget the epic left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` when the prefix is not 3-6 letters or a required field is blank, `conflict` when another epic already holds the prefix, and `limit-exceeded` at the board's epic cap.

signatures.signature: create_epic(prefix: str, title: str, description: str) -> EpicCreated

parameters.name: prefix
parameters.doc: 3-6 letters naming it. Upper-cased, it becomes the epic's id and the stem its issues are numbered from.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the body of work.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: What the epic covers, for a reader who has not seen its issues.

functions.name: create_issue
functions.brief: Create a self-contained, dispatchable issue, which a child agent can be briefed from.
functions.detail:
`in_scope`, `out_of_scope` and `completion_criteria` are what a child agent is briefed from, so they are written for a reader with no other context.

Returns: The id the board **assigned**, and the board budget the issue left behind. It is numbered under its epic's prefix (`AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2`, …), or under `ISSUE` when it has no epic, and keeping it is what blocks a later issue on this one or waits for it.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` when a required field is blank or `agent` or a reviewer is not one this agent may assign, `not-found` for an unknown epic or blocker, and `limit-exceeded` at the board's issue cap.

signatures.signature: create_issue(title: str, in_scope: str, out_of_scope: str, completion_criteria: str, agent: str, *, description: str | None = None, blocked_by: list[str] | None = None, epic_id: str | None = None, reviewers: list[str] | None = None) -> IssueCreated

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the work.

parameters.name: in_scope
parameters.doc: What the issue covers, precisely. Part of the brief a child agent is given.

parameters.name: out_of_scope
parameters.doc: What the issue deliberately does not cover, so the work stops where it was meant to.

parameters.name: completion_criteria
parameters.doc: What must be true for the issue to be done. It is what a reviewer checks the work against.

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent the issue is dispatched to. It must be one this agent may spawn.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: What the work is. Written for a child agent with no other context.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of every issue that must be done before this one. The default is none.

parameters.name: epic_id
parameters.doc: The id of an existing epic to group it under. The default leaves it ungrouped and numbered under `ISSUE`.

parameters.name: reviewers
parameters.doc: The agents that must approve the work, from the set this agent may spawn. Required when this run's reviewers feature is on.

functions.name: update_issue
functions.brief: Revise an issue; at least one field must be supplied.
functions.detail:
An argument left out is left alone. `description=None` empties the description and `epic_id=None` detaches the issue from its epic, which is why both default to `UNCHANGED` rather than to `None`.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` when no field was supplied or one was blanked, and `not-found` for an unknown issue or epic id.

signatures.signature: update_issue(id: str, *, title: str | None = None, description: str | None | Unchanged = UNCHANGED, in_scope: str | None = None, out_of_scope: str | None = None, completion_criteria: str | None = None, status: IssueStatus | None = None, epic_id: str | None | Unchanged = UNCHANGED) -> None

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to revise.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: The title to replace the old one with. The default keeps the one it has.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: The description to replace the old one with; `None` clears it, and the default keeps the one it has.

parameters.name: in_scope
parameters.doc: The scope statement to replace the old one with.

parameters.name: out_of_scope
parameters.doc: The non-scope statement to replace the old one with.

parameters.name: completion_criteria
parameters.doc: The completion criteria to replace the old ones with.

parameters.name: status
parameters.doc: Where the issue now stands. The default keeps the status it has.

parameters.name: epic_id
parameters.doc: The epic to regroup it under; `None` detaches it from the one it has, and the default keeps the grouping.

functions.name: set_issue_blocked_by
functions.brief: Replace an issue's whole blocker set; an empty list clears every blocker.
functions.detail: Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a blank id or blocker, `not-found` for an issue or blocker the board does not hold, and `conflict` when an edge would close a cycle or block the issue on itself.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue whose blockers to replace.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of every issue that must now be done before it. An empty list clears them all.

functions.name: remove_epic
functions.brief: Remove an epic, keeping its issues and ungrouping them.
functions.detail:
Returns: The board budget the removal left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The epic to remove.

functions.name: remove_issue
functions.brief: Remove an issue and every blocker edge pointing at it.
functions.detail:
Returns: The board budget the removal left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to remove.

functions.name: wait_for_issue
functions.brief: Register a wait on an issue, which suspends the agent between turns until it is terminal.
functions.detail:
Nothing blocks inside the program: the wait is recorded and the call returns at once, so the rest of the program still runs. The suspension happens after the program ends, between turns — the run frees this agent's slot until the issue is terminal, done or failed, then resumes on the next turn. It is how a turn's work is sequenced behind an issue it depends on. The issue this agent was assigned to implement is the one issue it may not wait on.

Returns: gg's acknowledgement that the wait is registered, which says what happens once the program ends.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a blank id, or for this agent's own assigned issue, `not-found` for an id the board does not hold, and `unavailable` when the run has no board.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to wait on. It may not be the issue this agent was assigned.

functions.name: add_task
functions.brief: Add a task to the task graph.
functions.detail:
`blocked_by` names the tasks that must finish before this one, and defaults to none.

Returns: The task budget the addition left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a blank id or title, `conflict` on a duplicate id or an edge that would close a cycle, `not-found` for an unknown blocker, and `limit-exceeded` at the task cap.

parameters.doc: The id chosen for it. Every other task call takes it, and no two tasks may share one.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the work.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: What the work is, at whatever length is useful.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of the tasks that must be done before this one. The default is none.

functions.name: update_task
functions.brief: Revise a task's title, description or status; at least one must be supplied.
functions.detail:
An argument left out is left alone. `description=None` empties the description, which is why it defaults to `UNCHANGED` rather than to `None`.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` when no field was supplied or one was blanked, and `not-found` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: title

parameters.name: description

parameters.name: status
parameters.doc: Where the task now stands. The default keeps the status it has.

functions.brief: Replace a task's whole blocker set; an empty list clears every blocker.
functions.detail: Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a blank id or blocker, `not-found` for a task or blocker that is not on the list, and `conflict` when an edge would close a cycle or block the task on itself.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task whose blockers to replace.

parameters.name: blocked_by

functions.name: complete_task
functions.brief: Mark a task done.
functions.detail:
Tasks it was blocking become actionable once every one of their blockers is done.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to mark done.

functions.name: remove_task
functions.brief: Remove a task and every blocker edge pointing at it.
functions.detail:
Returns: The task budget the removal left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to remove.

functions.name: write_memory
functions.brief: Record a durable memory that survives a context compaction.
functions.detail:
A memory may also carry **code**. `code` is a Python module whose public names are bound at `lib.<name>` in every later program this session writes, so a helper got right once is never written again; `on_use` is a script gg runs the first time the memory comes into use, whose views arrive on the next turn. Neither is context: they cost no window, are never shown back, and count against no body limit.

Returns: The memory budget the write left behind. A maximum this run does not bound is `None`, which is worth checking before subtracting.

Raises `ToolError`: `conflict` on a duplicate name, and `limit-exceeded` when the body would breach the run's caps — revising or deleting a memory is the way out, rather than accruing more.

signatures.signature: write_memory(name: str, description: str, body: str, *, code: str | None = None, on_use: str | None = None) -> MemoryUsage

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug: letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`. Every other memory call takes it, and no two memories may share one.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: A one-line description of what the memory holds. Where the run keeps a memory index this is the memory's line in it, and so all that is visible until it is read.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The memory's contents.

parameters.name: code
parameters.doc: A Python module whose public names are bound at `lib.<name>` for the rest of the session. The default records a memory that is only prose.

parameters.name: on_use
parameters.doc: A script gg runs the first time the memory comes into use. The default runs nothing.

functions.name: update_memory
functions.brief: Replace an existing memory's description and body, keyed on its slug.
functions.detail:
Its code and on-use script are replaced too — leaving them out clears them.

Returns: The memory budget the replacement left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` when no memory has that name.

signatures.signature: update_memory(name: str, description: str, body: str, *, code: str | None = None, on_use: str | None = None) -> MemoryUsage

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The slug of the memory to replace. Every other argument replaces what it held.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: The one-line description to replace the old one with.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The contents to replace the old ones with.

parameters.name: code
parameters.doc: The Python module to replace the old one with. The default clears it.

parameters.name: on_use
parameters.doc: The script to replace the old one with. The default clears it.

functions.name: create_memory
functions.brief: Record a new memory whose contents stay out of the context window until they are read.
functions.detail:
Returns: The memory budget the new memory left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a blank field or a slug with characters a name may not hold, `conflict` on a duplicate slug, and `limit-exceeded` when the contents, or the index entry, would breach a limit.

signatures.signature: create_memory(name: str, description: str, body: str, *, code: str | None = None, on_use: str | None = None) -> MemoryUsage

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug: letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`. No two memories may share one.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: A one-line description of what the memory holds. Required where the run keeps an index, since that is the memory's line in it.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The initial contents, which stay out of the context window until they are read.

parameters.name: code
parameters.doc: A Python module bound at `lib.<name>` once the memory is read. The default records a memory that is only prose.

parameters.name: on_use
parameters.doc: A script gg runs on that first read. The default runs nothing.

functions.name: read_memory
functions.brief: Read one memory's full contents by slug, which is the only thing that brings them into context.
functions.detail:
A memory that carries code loads that code on being read: the reply names the `lib.<key>` it is bound at, and it stays bound for the rest of the session.

Returns: The memory's body, and — where it carried code — the `lib.<key>` its public names are now bound at.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` when no memory has that slug.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

functions.name: edit_memory
functions.brief: Revise a memory in place, replacing the one exact occurrence of `search` with `replace`.
functions.detail:
Appending is done by quoting the last line and replacing it with itself plus what is being added.

Returns: The memory budget the revision left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` when the text does not appear, `conflict` when it appears more than once, `limit-exceeded` when the result would be too long, and `invalid-argument` when the edit would leave the memory empty — deleting it is the way to do that.

signatures.signature: edit_memory(name: str, search: str, replace: str) -> MemoryUsage

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The slug of the memory to revise.

parameters.name: search
parameters.doc: The exact text to find in its contents. It must appear exactly once.

parameters.name: replace
parameters.doc: The text to put in its place.

functions.name: search_memories
functions.brief: Find the memories mentioning any of `keywords`, best first.
functions.detail:
Plain case-insensitive substring matching over each memory's slug, description and contents, ranked by how many distinct keywords a memory mentions and then by how often. Several specific words rank better than one sentence; `read_memory` is what fetches a hit worth having in full.

Returns: The memories that matched, best first, each with an excerpt and the two counts it was ranked by. A search that matches nothing is an empty list.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` when every keyword is empty.

parameters.name: keywords
parameters.doc: The words to look for. Several specific words rank better than one sentence, because a memory is ranked by how many of them it mentions.

functions.name: delete_memory
functions.brief: Evict a memory by name, freeing room in the budget.
functions.detail:
Returns: The memory budget the eviction left behind.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` when no memory has that name.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

functions.name: open_file
functions.brief: Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and closable by it.
functions.detail:
The split from `files.read_file` is the point: reading gets bytes for the program, opening shows the file to the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them puts nothing in the window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

Returns: Exactly what `files.read_file` hands back for the same file, so the program holds the contents as well as the model holding the view.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for a missing path, and `invalid-argument` for an offset past the end of the file. The read is what fails; nothing is opened when it does.

signatures.signature: open_file(path: str, *, offset: int | None = None, limit: int | None = None) -> FileRead

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.doc: The 1-based line to start at.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.doc: How many lines to show from `offset`.

functions.name: open_text
functions.brief: Place a value the program computed into the context window, under `label`.
functions.detail:
A directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer, a table the program assembled. This is how the result of a program reaches the model that wrote it, and the only way it does. Opening the same label again replaces what it showed, so a program may refine a view in a loop without piling up a copy per iteration. Nothing is ever silently truncated.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for an empty label — a view with no selector could never be closed or attributed — and `limit-exceeded`, naming the cap, for a body or label over gg's caps.

parameters.name: label
parameters.doc: What to file the view under. `close` takes it, and opening the same label again replaces what it showed. It may not be empty.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: What to show. An empty body is allowed: it is how a program says that something it was showing is now empty.

functions.name: open_docs_view
functions.brief: Place one function's full documentation into the context window.
functions.detail:
Its signature, its description, and the declarations of any types it refers to that have not already been shown this session. This is how a function is read. It is a **view**, not a return value — the documentation arrives in the next prompt under a `Documentation` heading keyed by the function name, exactly as a file or a computed value arrives — so it is not available in the turn it is asked for. Ask in one turn, use it in the next. Opening the same function's documentation again replaces the view rather than adding a second copy, and `docs.close` closes it — not the `close` in this module, which does not reach documentation.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for an unknown or unbound name.

parameters.name: target
parameters.doc: The function to document: the function object itself (`files.read_file`), or the fully-qualified name its documentation is keyed by (`"gg.files.read_file"`). The bare name it is called by in its module (`"read_file"`) also resolves and is a fallback rather than the form to reach for: two modules are free to declare a `close`, and only the qualified name says which one is meant.

functions.name: close
functions.brief: Close every view carrying `selector`, freeing the tokens they occupied.
functions.detail:
Closing a file view forgets what was read, not what exists; closing a text view discards the only copy of what it held, so anything needed later belongs in a file or a memory first.

Documentation views are not reached from here. `docs.close` is what takes one away, and it is bought by a capability this call is not — so a sweep that included them would answer `0` for an agent that may not close one, which is indistinguishable from a selector that named nothing.

Returns: How many views were closed: for a file that is every page of that path, for a text view the one with that label, for the results of a search the label `search results`. A selector that is not open hands back `0` rather than failing, so a program that tidies up unconditionally need not guard every call.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for an empty selector, which names nothing rather than everything — no call here closes the window wholesale.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.doc: What the view is filed under: a file's path, a text view's label, or `search results`.

functions.name: current
functions.brief: List what is open in the context window right now.
functions.detail:
Reading it is what decides what to close when the window is filling up.

What it enumerates is the context window's contents, not any module's functions.

Returns: Each view's `kind`, the `selector` that closes it, roughly what it costs in `tokens`, and — for a paged file view — the `region` it covers.

functions.name: evict_file_view
functions.brief: Drop the contents of files that were read out of the context window.
functions.detail:
The files on disk are untouched: this forgets what was read, not what exists.

Returns: How many context items went and roughly how many tokens that reclaimed, with `paths` naming the files whose views were dropped.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a path that is given but empty; the default is how every file view is dropped.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file whose views to drop. The default drops every file view held.

functions.name: archive_thread
functions.brief: Move whole turns out of the context window.
functions.detail:
Every result carries a header with its turn number and roughly what holding it costs, which is what names the turns worth dropping: `context.archive_thread([TurnRange(4, 19)])` archives turns 4 through 19, both ends included. The agent's own messages in an archived turn are dropped; the results are kept and stay searchable with `search_archive`.

Returns: How many context items went and roughly how many tokens that reclaimed. `paths` is empty, since an archive drops turns rather than files.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for an empty list, too many spans at once, or a span that ends before it starts.

parameters.name: ranges
parameters.doc: The inclusive spans of turn numbers to move out of the window. They may overlap.

functions.name: search_archive
functions.brief: Search archived history for a case-insensitive substring, most recent first, up to 8 hits.
functions.detail:
`archive_empty` is worth checking before `hits`: it distinguishes "nothing has been archived yet" from "the search ran and matched nothing", so a program does not archive again believing the first archive failed.

Returns: The matches, most recent first and at most 8, beside the `archive_empty` flag.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for an empty query.

parameters.name: query
parameters.doc: The substring to look for. Matching is case-insensitive.

functions.name: compact
functions.brief: Compact the context window: the detailed thread is dropped and restarted from `summary`.
functions.detail:
A fresh read of each path in `files` is added to the restarted window. Skills, memories and the task list are kept as they are. gg asks for this call when the window is full, and refuses every other call until it arrives.

It does not stop the program: it registers the request and returns, and the rewrite happens once the program has ended. Everything not in the summary and not in `files` is gone, so the summary is written for the agent that comes after and `files` names what it will need in hand.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a blank summary. This is the one call gg does not refuse while a compaction is in flight, since nothing else can clear the window.

signatures.signature: compact(summary: str, files: list[str] | None = None) -> None

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What the restarted window opens with. Everything not in it and not re-read from `files` is gone.

parameters.name: files
parameters.doc: The paths to read afresh into the restarted window. The default reads nothing back.

functions.name: spawn_subagent
functions.brief: Delegate scoped work to a child agent, which runs in parallel while the program continues.
functions.detail:
`agent` names one of the agent profiles this agent may spawn — the system prompt lists them, and the profile selects the child's model, tools and instructions. The brief is exactly one of `prompt` and `issue_id`. The child shares the workspace.

Returns: The child's handle: the id `wait_for_subagents` and `send_message` take, the agent profile it runs as, and the model bound to that profile.

Raises `ToolError`: `limit-exceeded` at the delegation depth cap, and `invalid-argument` when `agent` is not one this agent may spawn.

signatures.signature: spawn_subagent(agent: str, *, prompt: str | None = None, issue_id: str | None = None) -> SubagentHandle

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent profile to run the child as, from the ones this agent may spawn. It selects the child's model, tools and instructions.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: Self-contained instructions for the child. Give this or `issue_id`, never both and never neither.

parameters.name: issue_id
parameters.doc: The board issue to brief the child from. Give this or `prompt`, never both and never neither.

functions.name: wait_for_subagents
functions.brief: Block until the named children have finished and collect their results in dispatch order.
functions.detail:
The default waits for every outstanding child. The run's wall-clock budget keeps running throughout, so one wait for many children costs far less than one wait per child.

Returns: One result per child, in dispatch order, each carrying its final message and how it ended. A child that produced no return value at all has no `status`.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for an id this agent did not spawn.

parameters.name: ids
parameters.doc: The children to wait for, as `spawn_subagent` returned them. The default waits for every one still outstanding.

functions.name: send_message
functions.brief: Deliver a message to a running child agent's inbox, which it reads at its next turn.
functions.detail: Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` for an unknown agent id, and `conflict` when that child has already returned.

parameters.name: agent_id
parameters.doc: The child to deliver to, as `spawn_subagent` returned it.

parameters.name: message
parameters.doc: What to put in its inbox. It reads it at its next turn.

functions.name: transition_state
functions.brief: Move the process this session is running inside on to another of its states.
functions.detail:
The state is named the way an agent to spawn is named. It is bound only when a state machine is driving the session and the current state has somewhere to go. Like `context.compact` it is registered rather than performed: the call validates the target, returns, and the program runs on to its end, because replacing the agent — and its window — mid-program would pull every remaining call out from under it. The first declaration in a turn is the one that stands.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a state this session may not move to, `refused` for a second declaration in one turn, and `unavailable` when this agent is not running inside a state machine at all.

signatures.signature: transition_state(state: str, note: str | None = None) -> None

parameters.name: state
parameters.doc: The state to move on to, named the way an agent to spawn is named.

parameters.name: note
parameters.doc: The opening message the next state's agent sees. The default tells it nothing.

functions.name: exec
functions.brief: Continue this session as a different agent, from the next turn.
functions.detail:
The named agent takes over with its own model, tools and instructions, keeping every capability the two of them share — the whole conversation above all, so it needs no catching up. Registered rather than performed, exactly as `transition_state` is and for the same reason: the window would otherwise be pulled out from under the program still composing into it. A session makes one succession per turn. It is bound only when this agent may make agent transitions and has agents it may become, and never while a state machine is driving the session.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for an agent this session may not become, `refused` for a second succession in one turn, and `unavailable` when this agent is running inside a machine, which is left by `transition_state` instead.

signatures.signature: exec(agent: str, prompt: str | None = None) -> None

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent to become, from the ones this agent may become.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: Its opening message. It already has the whole conversation, so this is the instruction rather than a briefing. The default tells it nothing.

functions.name: fork
functions.brief: Run a copy of this agent, in parallel, on something it will not do itself.
functions.detail:
The copy has the same model, the same tools and a private copy of the whole conversation, so `prompt` is the *difference* rather than a briefing — everything already worked out is already there.

The copy itself starts once this turn's tool results are recorded, because the conversation it inherits has to be a complete one. So `wait_for_subagents` can only collect it on a later turn, and waiting on it in the program that made it never returns it.

Returns: The copy's handle, carrying the id a later wait collects it by.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a blank prompt, `limit-exceeded` at the delegation depth cap, and `unavailable` when the run has no delegation runtime to copy this agent into.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: What the copy is to do instead. It has the whole conversation already, so this is the difference rather than a briefing.

functions.name: read_skill
functions.brief: Read a skill from the run's authored library, by name.
functions.detail:
Reading it also pins that body permanently into context, so a skill that has been read stays read.

A skill may be **code** rather than prose, or as well as it. Code is bound at `lib.<key>` for the rest of the session and the reply names the key and what it offers. An on-use script runs once this program has ended, and whatever it shows arrives on the next turn.

Returns: The skill's body with its front matter stripped, and — where the skill is code — the `lib.<key>` its public names are now bound at.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` — listing the skills that do exist — when the name is unknown.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The skill's name, as the system prompt lists it.

functions.name: history
functions.brief: List the programs this session has already run, oldest first.
functions.detail:
It lists shapes, not sources: `get` is what fetches one. The list survives a compaction, so it is also how a program whose text has left the context window is found again.

Returns: One summary per program already run, oldest first: the turn it ran on, how big it was, and whether it ran to its end. A session that has run nothing yet gets an empty list.

Raises `ToolError`: `unavailable` when this agent keeps no program library, which is a different fact from an empty one.

functions.name: get
functions.brief: Fetch the exact source of one program that ran; the default fetches the most recent.
functions.detail:
This is the first half of fixing a program without rewriting it: get what ran, patch it with ordinary string work — `replace`, an f-string, a regular expression — and hand the result to `rerun`. What comes back is the program that **executed**, so when a turn's program was itself handed over by `rerun`, the program that ran is what arrives rather than the few lines that asked for it, and fetch-patch-run composes turn after turn.

Returns: The source of the program that ran on that turn, as a string.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found`, naming the turns that are held, for a turn that ran no program or one old enough that the library has dropped it, and `unavailable` when this agent keeps no program library.

parameters.name: turn
parameters.doc: The turn whose program to fetch, as `history` reports it. The default fetches the most recent one.

functions.name: rerun
functions.brief: Hand gg a program to run in place of this one.
functions.detail:
The calling program finishes, then gg runs `source` as this turn's program. Used with `get` it fixes a program without re-emitting it. Nothing is undone: every call the calling program already made stands, and the program that runs next sees the world it left behind — so the hand-over belongs before work that should not happen twice.

The first call stands, because a silently replaced program is a change nobody can see. If the calling program then raises, the hand-over is cancelled along with everything else that program decided, and the turn ends in an ordinary error. Chains are bounded: one hand-over per turn, and the fixed program is the one that does the work.

Raises `ToolError`: `refused` for a second hand-over in one turn, `invalid-argument` for a blank source, and `unavailable` when this agent keeps no program library.

parameters.name: source
parameters.doc: The program to run in place of this one, as Python. It may not be blank.

functions.name: finish
functions.brief: End the session, reporting what was done in a sentence or two.
functions.detail:
This is the only thing that ends a working agent's session. It does not stop the program — whatever follows it still runs — so it belongs last, once the tools have confirmed the work is really done. A program that then fails has the ending cancelled and gets another turn.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` for a blank summary, and `unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What was done, in a sentence or two.

functions.name: approve
functions.brief: Accept the work under review: it meets every completion criterion and stays in scope.
functions.detail:
This ends the session. It does not stop the program — whatever follows it still runs — so it belongs last, once the change has actually been read. It takes nothing, because an approval carries no obligation beyond itself.

Raises `ToolError`: `unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

functions.name: request_changes
functions.brief: Reject the work under review, listing every change that must be made before acceptance.
functions.detail:
This ends the session, and does not stop the program. Each item says what is wrong and what to change.

Raises `ToolError`: `invalid-argument` when the list is empty, and `unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

parameters.name: items
parameters.doc: Every change that must be made before the work can be accepted, one per entry: what is wrong, and what to change. It may not be empty.

functions.name: wait
functions.brief: Register a wait on this issue, which suspends the agent between turns until it is terminal.
functions.detail:
`wait_for_issue` with the id already supplied, for the common case where the issue was just created and the next turn's work is sequenced behind it.

Returns: gg's acknowledgement that the wait is registered, which says what happens once the program ends.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` when the issue has since been removed.

functions.name: read
functions.brief: Read this memory's full contents, which a search hit does not carry.
functions.detail:
`read_memory` with the slug already supplied, for the common case where the search that found the memory is the thing in hand.

Returns: The memory's body, and — where it carried code — the `lib.<key>` its public names are now bound at.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` when the memory has since been deleted.

functions.name: close
functions.brief: Close this view, freeing the tokens it occupied.
functions.detail:
`views.close` with the selector already supplied, which is what lets a window be tidied by iterating over what is in it rather than by writing a selector out per view.

A documentation view is the one this does not take away, for the reason `views.close` does not: `docs.close` is the call for one of those, and it is bought by a capability this one is not.

Returns: How many views were closed, which for one page of a paged file is every page of that path.

functions.name: send
functions.brief: Deliver a message to this child's inbox, which it reads at its next turn.
functions.detail:
`send_message` with the id already supplied, for the common case where the handle the spawn returned is still in hand.

Raises `ToolError`: `conflict` when this child has already returned.

parameters.name: message
parameters.doc: What to put in its inbox.

functions.name: source
functions.brief: Fetch this program's source, which a summary does not carry.
functions.detail:
`get` with the turn already supplied, for the common case where the directory entry that named the program is the thing in hand.

Returns: The source of the program that ran on that turn, as a string.

Raises `ToolError`: `not-found` when the library has since dropped that turn.

    IN_PROGRESS
    DONE
types.brief: Where a task stands.

members.name: PENDING
members.brief: Not started. Every task begins here.

members.name: IN_PROGRESS
members.brief: Being worked on now.

members.name: DONE
members.brief: Finished. Tasks blocked on it become actionable once all their blockers are done.

types.name: MemoryUsage
types.declaration:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MemoryUsage:
    count: int
    max_count: int | None
    total_chars: int
    max_total_chars: int | None
    index_chars: int | None
    max_index_chars: int | None
types.brief: How much of the run's durable-memory budget is used, after the call that returned it.
types.detail: Every maximum is optional: each limit can be turned off, and a run's memory strategy applies only some of them, so `None` means nothing bounds that axis — which is worth checking before subtracting.

members.name: count
members.brief: Memories currently held.

members.name: max_count
members.brief: The most memories this run allows, if it limits the count.

members.name: total_chars
members.brief: Characters of body currently held, across all memories.

members.name: max_total_chars
members.brief: The most characters of body this run allows in total, if it limits the aggregate.

members.name: index_chars
members.brief: Characters the memory index occupies, under a run that keeps one.

members.name: max_index_chars
members.brief: The most characters the index may occupy, if it is limited.

types.name: MemoryHit

class MemoryHit:

members.name: name

members.name: description
members.brief: Its description, or the empty string when it was created without one.

members.name: matched
members.brief: How many distinct keywords it matched — the primary ranking.

members.name: occurrences
members.brief: How many times those keywords occur in it — the tiebreak.

members.name: excerpt
members.brief: A short window of the memory around its first match.

memberFunctions.name: read
memberFunctions.brief: Read this memory's full contents, which a search hit does not carry.

types.name: ViewKind
types.declaration:
class ViewKind(Enum):
    FILE
    TEXT
    DOCS
types.brief: Which of the three kinds a view is.
types.detail: The taxonomy is closed at three deliberately: everything on disk is a file, everything a program can compute is a string, and documentation is neither — gg holds it.

members.name: FILE
members.brief: A file that was opened; its selector is the path.

members.name: TEXT
members.brief: A computed value; its selector is the label it was given.

members.name: DOCS
members.brief: A function's documentation; its selector is the function's name.

types.name: ViewRegion
types.brief: The window of lines a paged file view covers; absent for a whole-file view.

members.name: offset
members.brief: The 1-based first line the view shows.

members.name: limit
members.brief: How many lines it shows.

types.name: OpenView
types.brief: One view open in the context window, as `current` reports it.

members.name: kind
members.brief: Whether it is a file, text, or documentation view.

members.name: selector
members.brief: What closes it.
members.detail: A file's path, a text view's label or `search results` for `close`, and for a documentation view the key `docs.close` takes.

members.name: tokens
members.brief: Roughly what holding it costs, in tokens.

members.name: region
members.brief: The line window a paged file view covers; `None` for a whole-file view and for text views.

memberFunctions.name: close
memberFunctions.brief: Close this view, freeing the tokens it occupied.

types.name: ReclaimReport
types.brief: What a context reclaim actually freed from the live context window.

members.name: items
members.brief: Context items dropped from the live window.

members.name: reclaimed_tokens
members.brief: Approximately how many tokens that freed.

members.name: paths
members.brief: The workspace paths whose views were evicted. Empty for an archive.

members.name: detail
members.brief: The prose summary of what was reclaimed.

types.name: TurnRange
types.brief: An inclusive span of turn numbers, the unit `archive_thread` moves out of the window.
types.detail: The numbers are the ones on the header of every result, so `TurnRange(4, 19)` means exactly the turns numbered 4 through 19 — both ends included.

members.name: start
members.brief: The first turn in the span.

members.name: end
members.brief: The last turn in the span, inclusive.

types.name: AgentEnding
types.declaration:
class AgentEnding(Enum):
    COMPLETED
    EXHAUSTED
    TIMED_OUT
    MODEL_ERROR
    AUTH_ERROR
    LIMIT_EXCEEDED
types.brief: How a child agent's loop ended — gg's own six words, as the tool-calling path reports them.

members.name: COMPLETED
members.brief: It finished normally, calling `session.finish`, and its summary is what it returned.

members.name: EXHAUSTED
members.brief: It reached the per-run turn ceiling.

members.name: TIMED_OUT
members.brief: It passed its wall-clock deadline.

members.name: MODEL_ERROR
members.brief: A model turn failed.

members.name: AUTH_ERROR
members.brief: The run's credential was refused.

members.name: LIMIT_EXCEEDED
members.brief: An execution ceiling stopped it — consecutive errors, error rate, or cost.

types.name: SubagentResult
types.brief: One child agent's collected result.

members.name: id
members.brief: The child's id.

members.name: status

members.name: summary
members.brief: Its final message.

types.name: ProgramSummary
types.declaration:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProgramSummary:
    turn: int
    lines: int
    chars: int
    ok: bool
    error: str | None
types.brief: One program that already ran, as `history` lists it.
types.detail: It describes the program's **shape**, never its source: a directory that inlined every program would put the whole session back in the context window, which is the one thing the library exists to avoid. `get` is what fetches a source.

members.name: turn
members.brief: The turn it ran on — what `get` takes.

members.name: lines
members.brief: How many lines of source it was.

members.name: chars
members.brief: How many characters of source it was.

members.name: ok
members.brief: Whether it ran to its end, with nothing raised and no sandbox ceiling stopping it.

members.name: error
members.brief: The error it ended with, when it did not run to its end; `None` when it did.

memberFunctions.name: source
memberFunctions.brief: Fetch this program's source, which a summary does not carry.

types.name: ToolErrorCode
types.declaration:
class ToolErrorCode(Enum):
    INVALID_ARGUMENT
    NOT_FOUND
    CONFLICT
    REFUSED
    UNAVAILABLE
    LIMIT_EXCEEDED
    IO_ERROR
    OTHER
types.brief: Why a gg call failed — the `code` a handler branches on rather than the message it reads.

members.name: INVALID_ARGUMENT
members.brief: The arguments were malformed, ill-typed, or out of range.
members.detail: It covers a path that is absolute or climbs out of the workspace, and an agent name this run does not declare.

members.name: NOT_FOUND
members.brief: The named thing does not exist.
members.detail: A file, a skill, a memory, a task, an epic, an issue, a subagent, a stored program, or a documentation entry.

members.name: CONFLICT
members.brief: Well-formed, but in conflict with the current state.
members.detail: An ambiguous edit, a dependency cycle, a duplicate id, a subagent that has already returned.

members.name: REFUSED
members.brief: gg refused the call on a rule about the session's state.
members.detail: A compaction in flight that this call is not the one it asked for, a memory call while memories are read-only, a second ending or hand-over in a turn that already declared one, or a hook that blocked it. A ceiling that was reached is `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` rather than this.

members.name: UNAVAILABLE
members.brief: The call exists and this run's capability set does not offer it.
members.detail: A withheld call is refused by gg rather than hidden, so this is what reaching for one raises.

members.name: LIMIT_EXCEEDED
members.brief: A gg-side ceiling was reached.
members.detail: A shell timeout, a store cap, the delegation depth cap, one of the view caps a program spends, or the run's wall-clock budget.

members.name: IO_ERROR
members.brief: The underlying input, output or process failed.

members.name: OTHER
members.brief: The failure was not classified.
members.detail: Reserved for outcomes raised outside a tool implementation; no call in this SDK produces it.

types.name: ToolError
types.brief: A gg call that failed.

members.name: tool
members.brief: The gg call that failed, under gg's own name for it (`read_file`, `spawn_subagent`).
members.detail: It is gg's name for the capability rather than this SDK's spelling of it, so it is the same word in every language a program may be written in.

members.name: code
members.brief: The failure class, so a handler branches on a value rather than on prose.

types.name: Unchanged
types.declaration:
class Unchanged(Enum):
    UNCHANGED
types.brief: The value that leaves a patch field exactly as it is.
types.detail: A field a patch may also *clear* has three states rather than two, and Python already spells "absent" as `None` — which here is the request to clear it. So the third state gets a name of its own: leave the argument out (or pass `UNCHANGED`) to keep what is there, pass `None` to empty it, pass a value to replace it. A field with no clear state is an ordinary `X | None = None`, where `None` simply means it is not being changed.

members.name: UNCHANGED
members.brief: The only member; `UNCHANGED` is the name a program writes.
